Empirical Research Plan – Skill Portability, Occupational Choice and Wage Growth  
==========================================================================  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Chosen strategy:  Two–stage least-squares (2SLS) event-study focused on workers displaced by plausibly exogenous plant closures.

Rationale  
•  Plant closures provide a shock that forces workers to look for new jobs and often new occupations; the separation is largely unrelated to individual productivity.  
•  Whether a displaced worker lands in an occupation that is “similar” (high task overlap) or “distant” (low task overlap) is strongly affected by the local stock of vacancies in related occupations.  
•  We therefore instrument the realised task–similarity of the post-displacement occupation with the employment share of task-related occupations in the worker’s local labour market (commuting zone) in the year of displacement – a Bartik/shift-share style instrument.  
•  The second stage relates task similarity (treatment intensity) to subsequent wage paths, producing causal estimates of the wage return to partially transferable skills.  
•  Because wages are observed annually before and after the shock, we embed the IV in an event-time difference-in-differences framework to obtain dynamic treatment effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
   Tisr = Task-similarity index between the pre-closure occupation i and the first post-closure occupation, normalised to the [0,1] range. We also create a binary “High-Similarity” indicator =1 if Tisr ≥ 0.75 (top quartile) for ease of interpretation.

Instrument  
   Zisr = Employment share of occupations with T ≥ 0.75 relative to i in region r and year s (the “related-occupation share”) measured just before displacement.  

Control group / counterfactual  
   Displaced workers who move into low-similarity (bottom quartile) occupations provide the counterfactual wage path. Because the instrument varies continuously, we estimate both continuous and binary 2SLS.  

Treatment timing / event date  
   τ = 0 in the calendar year of the plant-closure separation. Outcomes are followed for k = –5,…,+10 years.  

Sample definition  
   • Male West-German workers entering the labour market 1975–1995.  
   • Experience a plant closure between 1980–1998 (identified in the social-security data when *all* employees of plant p exit within a 12-month window).  
   • First post-closure job starts within 12 months.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1.  Exogeneity of plant closures  
    Closure probability is orthogonal to the displaced worker’s unobserved productivity.  – Plausible: closures are generally driven by technology or demand shocks, not individual workers. We exclude single-worker plants and control for pre-closure plant wage levels to bolster this.

A2.  Relevance of the instrument  
    Local related-occupation share strongly predicts the realised task-similarity of the post-closure job.  – Very plausible given German occupational labour-market segmentation.

A3.  Exclusion (instrument affects wages only through task similarity)  
    Conditional on region-year fixed effects and local labour-market controls, variation in the share of related occupations affects wages solely via the occupation entered, not through other channels. – Reasonable but we test for violations (e.g., by showing no pre-trend correlation with wages).

A4.  Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA)  
    One worker’s treatment does not change others’ outcomes in the 2 % sample – plausible.

A5.  Common pre-trends (for the DID dimension)  
    Absent differences in task similarity, high- and low-similarity groups would have parallel wage paths pre-closure – testable in the data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Endogenous regional demand shocks – regions with booming related occupations may also have higher wage growth.  
   • Include commuting-zone × calendar-year fixed effects and region-specific linear trends.  
   • Placebo on non-displaced workers in the same region to confirm no direct wage effect of the instrument.

Threat 2: Measurement error in task similarity (Tisr) – could attenuate estimates.  
   • Construct similarity matrix from two independent BIBB waves; use leave-one-out averages; check robustness to alternative similarity cut-offs.

Threat 3: Selective migration – high-ability workers may move regions before or after closure.  
   • Limit sample to workers who stay in the same commuting zone for at least two years pre- and post-closure.  
   • Re-estimate including movers and instrument migration with pre-closure home ownership rate as a robustness check.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# -------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE & IV
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
# -------------------------------------------------------
admin  <- fread("social_security_spells.csv")  # spell-level admin data
tasks  <- fread("task_similarity_matrix.csv")  # 64x64 similarity

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct analysis sample
# -------------------------------------------------------
# (a) Flag plant closures
admin[, plant_exit := .N, by = .(plant_id, exit_year)]
admin[, closure := (plant_exit == .N) & (.N >= 5), by = plant_id]      # 5+ workers plant
admin[, displaced := closure & (spell_end_reason == "layoff")]

# (b) Keep first closure event per worker
admin[, first_disp := min(spell_end_date[displaced==TRUE]), by = worker_id]
sample <- admin[exit_date == first_disp]   # one obs per displaced worker

# (c) Map occupations to similarity matrix
setkey(tasks, occ_from, occ_to)
sample[, sim := tasks[.(pre_occ, post_occ), similarity]]

# (d) Instrument: related-occ share in CZ-year
occ_cz <- admin[ , .N, by = .(cz, year, occ2d)]
occ_cz <- merge(occ_cz, tasks[, .(pre_occ = occ_from, occ2d = occ_to, high_rel = (similarity>=0.75))],
                by = "occ2d", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
occ_cz <- occ_cz[high_rel==TRUE,
                 .(rel_share = sum(N)/sum(N)), by = .(cz, year, pre_occ)]
sample <- merge(sample, occ_cz, by.x = c("cz", "disp_year", "pre_occ"),
                              by.y = c("cz", "year", "pre_occ"), all.x = TRUE)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Create event-time panel (−5…+10) of wages
# -------------------------------------------------------
panel <- admin[worker_id %in% sample$worker_id]
panel <- merge(panel, sample[,.(worker_id, disp_year)], by="worker_id")
panel[, rel_year := year - disp_year]
panel <- panel[rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 10]

# Wage variable (real, top-coded)
panel[, log_wage := log(pmin(wage, ceiling_ss_contrib))]
panel[, high_sim := (sim >= 0.75)]   # binary treatment

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 4. 2SLS event-study
# -------------------------------------------------------
est <- feols(log_wage ~ i(rel_year, high_sim, ref = -1) |                     # 2nd stage
                         i(rel_year, rel_share, ref = -1) ~ 
                         0 | worker_id + cz*year,                             # fixed effects
             data = panel)
summary(est)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: leave-one-out Bartik instrument
# -------------------------------------------------------
# Exclude worker’s own plant from occ_cz counts, rebuild rel_share_loo
# Re-estimate est replacing rel_share with rel_share_loo

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Plot dynamic effects
# -------------------------------------------------------
coef_df <- as.data.frame(est, type="confint")
ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = rel_year, y = Estimate)) +
    geom_line() + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=CI_low, ymax=CI_high), alpha=.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
    theme_minimal() + ylab("Log-wage effect: high vs low similarity")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory predicts that wages fall upon displacement but recover faster when the new occupation uses similar tasks because partially transferable skills retain their value.  

Prior:  
• Initial wage loss at τ = 0 of −10 % for high-similarity movers vs −20 % for low-similarity movers.  
• By τ = 5, the gap closes to ≈ 6 pp, implying roughly 40-50 % of post-displacement wage growth is attributable to partially transferable skills.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ....................... 1  
C2: Exogeneity of instrument .............................. 0.8  
C3: Parallel pre-trends (checked graphically) ............. 1  
C4: No defiers / monotonicity ............................. 0.8  
C5: SUTVA, no spillovers in 2 % sample .................... 1  

Overall: 4.6 / 5 – solid but hinges on exclusion restriction and migration selection.
